title: Madison is buying part of an old farm with the goal of building more housing
text: Wisconsin Public Radio (WPR) Logo Donate Icon Donate Search wpr.org Search Icon Economy , Housing , News Madison is buying part of an old farm with the goal of building more housing Former Voit farm property is being redeveloped as a housing subdivision on Madison's east side The city of Madison is purchasing part of an old farm site with the goal of turning the land into housing.  Madison’s Common Council recently OK’d an agreement authorizing the city to spend $4.3 million to acquire four parcels of land, totaling about three acres from what was once known as the Voit family farm. The deal included a 90-day due-diligence period, specifying that the final sale is contingent on inspections and any necessary environmental clean-up to be completed by the seller. The land once housed a fertilizer plant, and it’s part of an area that’s long been eyed as a site for more housing, said Madison’s Planning & Community Economic Development Director Matt Wachter. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. The four parcels are on Madison’s east side at Walter Street, Chicago Avenue and Canvas Road, near Cottage Grove Road. “The mission is to add housing in these places that you know really makes sense,” Wachter said in an interview with WPR. “Cottage Grove Road has transit. You’re right next to a library. You’re right next to a bunch of amenities that people value.” Construction on the soon-to-be-acquired parcels could start in 2027, Wachter said. He said it hasn’t yet been determined whether the city will partner with an outside development company or whether that work will be done in-house through Madison’s Community Development Authority. He expects the area will include a mix of owner-occupied and rental properties, some of which will be subsidized and some of which will available at market rates. At least of some of the new homes are likely to be townhomes, he said. “What we call missing middle housing types,” Wachter said. “So things that are bigger than a single-family home but not full on large apartment buildings.” Madison is buying the land from the Starkweather development company, a partnership between Stone House Development and Threshold Development. Starkweather previously bought a total of 60 acres from the Voit family for over $8 million. Since then, Starkweather has been using tax incentives from the city to develop housing on a large chunk of the property. “For a variety of reasons, development really kind of slowed down out there, and the developer decided that they wanted to get out of the property, and the remaining, you know, three or four development pads are out there,” Wachter said. “We looked at it and said, ‘This really actually meets a lot of the city’s goals for our land banking program.’” Starkweather did not respond to an inquiry from WPR. During a meeting in June, Stone House Development President Helen Bradbury told Madison’s Common Council that about 30 acres of the former Voit Farm property could be used for housing while the rest makes sense as a “beautiful pond and nature space.” Once it’s fully developed, she said the entire project could include nearly 1,000 units of housing. During that meeting, Alder Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford said the project would increase housing supply in an area where it’s sorely needed. “(This is) in an area that has high rents and has very little affordable housing available,” said Martinez-Rutherford, whose district includes the former Voit farm property. Madison has seen some of the steepest population growth in Wisconsin, and many residents say they struggle to find housing they can afford. To ease the shortage, Madison city officials have set a goal of adding 15,000 new homes to the city’s supply by 2030. title: Wisconsin police shooting of Corey Ruiz sparks protests and investigation
text: Sections About Connect With Us 1  /  0  (CNN)- Authorities in Wisconsin are investigating a fatal police shooting in Madison that has prompted protests and renewed calls for transparency. Community members gathered Thursday for a vigil honoring Corey Ruiz, who was shot and killed by police Wednesday at the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets. According to Madison police, four officers responded to the scene, where Ruiz allegedly injured one officer with a knife during a struggle before officers opened fire. The Wisconsin Department of Justice’s Division of Criminal Investigation has taken over the case, which is being investigated as an active homicide inquiry. Once the investigation is complete, the findings will be turned over to the local district attorney’s office to determine whether any charges are warranted. As demonstrators rallied in downtown Madison, Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers and city leaders called for a transparent review of the incident. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said no one should lose their life during an encounter with law enforcement, regardless of their background or past. All four officers involved in the shooting have been placed on administrative leave while the investigation continues. Madison Police Chief John Patterson acknowledged the strain the incident has placed on the community, saying the use of force can erode public trust and emphasizing the importance of a thorough, independent review. Corey Ruiz, who was in his 30s and a member of the Madison community, was killed Wednesday, officials said during a news conference Thursday. He was shot after he pulled out a knife during a struggle with four officers, police said.​ The news conference became heated, as Madison Police Chief John Patterson was interrupted by two protesters for about 20 minutes. One took over the microphone to condemn police brutality and demand the officer responsible be jailed. Patterson described the case as “an open and active homicide investigation.” Madison police shoot man they say was wielding a knife The state Justice Department’s Criminal Investigation Division is leading the investigation and will release the name of the officer who fired his weapon, he said. The mayor also called for answers about Ruiz’s shooting. “I want to be clear: It does not matter who you are or what your past is. You should not lose your life as a result of an encounter with law enforcement. That should not happen,” Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said Thursday, promising that the shooting will be “rigorously investigated.” Wisconsin public records show that Ruiz had 40 misdemeanor and felony convictions from 2009 to 2025. The crimes include robbery by force, strangulation, drug possession, vehicle theft and battery of a public safety worker, according to the records. It appears that Ruiz was most recently convicted of resisting law enforcement and drug paraphernalia possession, the records show. Jazzman Brown, a community organizer in Madison, said Ruiz was a father who was experiencing homelessness and mental health struggles. “Corey I’ve known for 20-plus years. He was a friend of my brother’s. We went to school together. He dated my best friend at one point. We’ve just known each other forever,” Brown said. She remembered Ruiz as a “loving” person and “the life of the party” who “filled the room with energy whenever he was in it.” “A father, a son, a friend, a loved one, and he’s gone. And his kids, his mom, his entire family, everyone that loved him and knew him, watched him be murdered in cold blood,” she added. Brown organized a vigil for Thursday night to honor his memory. “He didn’t deserve to be gunned down in front of the world, and he has people who love him. And he’s more than just a case number. ... We can’t just continue to let this problem go on. There has to be some kind of change,” Brown said. Efforts to reach Ruiz’s family members were not immediately successful Thursday. The shooting unfolded Wednesday afternoon when police officers were dispatched to Madison’s Marquette neighborhood after reports of someone stealing bicycles and checking vehicle doors, police said in their initial statement. ​Officers located Ruiz, but he biked off, traveling through backyards to get away, authorities said. Police found him shortly afterward at the intersection of South Baldwin and Williamson streets, police said. Ruiz either fell or was pulled off the bicycle, police said, and then a struggle with officers ensued in the intersection. During the struggle, Ruiz pulled out a fixed-blade knife and injured an officer, police said.​ A makeshift memorial for Corey Ruiz in Madison, Wis., on Thursday. Mark Hoffman / Milwaukee Journal / USA Today Network via Reuters Police said that a stun gun was used, but that it was ineffective. The officer who was injured with the knife then fired at Ruiz, police said. None of the four officers who were detaining the man wore body cameras. Videos of the shooting were captured by bystanders and went viral on social media. One of them, verified by NBC News, appears to show officers holding the man as someone yells, “Let go!” Multiple shouts of “He’s got a knife!” can also be heard.​ Someone then appears to yell, “Taser!” Roughly three seconds later, a male officer standing over Ruiz appears to fire three rounds, and Ruiz stops moving.​ Four officers were involved in or witnessed this shooting, according to police. Only one officer, who is considered a veteran officer, fired his weapon, police said. He has not yet been publicly identified. All of the officers involved will be placed on administrative leave pending an independent investigation by the Wisconsin Department of Criminal Investigation, as required under state law. Police said that lifesaving measures were performed at the scene and that Ruiz was pronounced dead later at the hospital. Aeiramique Glass, the interim independent monitor with the city whose sector monitors the police department, told NBC News the agency is conducting an investigation into the shooting but hasn’t gotten much from the department so far. She recalled rushing to the scene Wednesday and holding crying witnesses in her arms. “What we all seen was a man be shot in his head while he was laying on the floor after he was Tased, and after he was shot in the head three times,” Glass said about the video of the fatal shooting. “We have a situation where, regardless of all of the details surrounding it, his death could have been prevented,” Glass said. “We know there is a better way.” Demonstrators on Thursday at the intersection where Corey Ruiz was killed in Madison. The shooting took place in an area with a history of police killings. It was a block and a half from where Tony Robinson was shot and killed by a Madison officer in 2015 and near the site where Paul Heenan was shot and killed by a police officer in Madison in 2012, the chief said. Hundreds gathered Thursday evening at the scene of the shooting, where heads were bowed for a moment of silence followed by chants of “Say his name! title: Police killing of homeless man roils capital city of Wisconsin | News , Sports , Jobs
text: Jul 24, 2026 Protesters march after a Madison police officer shot and killed a man Wednesday, July 22, 2026, in Madison, Wis. (AP Photo/Kayla Wolf) MADISON, Wis. (AP) — Protesters burst into a Thursday news conference about the police shooting of a homeless man in Madison, taking the microphone from the police chief and arguing with some attendees who said they wanted to hear more about the investigation. The group of roughly 20 protesters burst into the room at the Madison police station, shortly after Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway and Common Council President Sabrina Madison identified the man killed by police as Corey Durell Ruiz, a homeless resident. Ruiz, 38, was shot and killed Wednesday after police said he resisted arrest and injured an officer with a knife. Police Chief John Patterson stepped away from the microphone when the protesters were shouting, and one man in the group took his spot at the podium. The event quickly devolved into a shouting match. One protester held a sign saying “Corrupt cops deserve to die too!!!” Moments earlier, the mayor said the shooting will be “rigorously investigated.” “It does not matter who you are or what your past is, you should not lose your life as a result of an encounter with law enforcement,” Satya Rhodes-Conway said. Madison, for her part, said “Corey could have been my brother because my brother is homeless and he often rides a bike.” Court records show Ruiz had been in and out of jail over the past decade on charges including failing to pay child support, driving a vehicle without consent, jumping bail, threatening authorities, taking a vehicle without consent, possessing drug paraphernalia, resisting an officer and retail theft. “He’s a human being. He had a family. He has parents who loved him who brought him home, who cared for him,” Madison said, adding that she’s struggling to understand what she’s seen in videos of the shooting that have circulated on social media. “My first thought is, when the officer’s walking away, why isn’t he walking away in cuffs,” Madison said. “I’m angry, there’s no way around it.” Once the protesters quieted down, the chief resumed his presentation, promising his department’s full cooperation with the state investigation. The shooting has roiled Wisconsin’s capital city, with Gov. Tony Evers calling for “transparency and accountability” and Madison community members gathering Thursday at a growing memorial. None of the four officers who were detaining the man wore body cameras, but passersby recorded the confrontation on video, and accused the officers of overreacting. “I thought, ‘Holy cow — what could have warranted that?’ It looked to me like they had him under control,” David Ortiz-Whittingham, who saw officers swarming and heard the gunshots, said Thursday. “Even now, knowing about the knife, did he have to die for it? Could this have been de-escalated without him losing his life?” The police chief released few details Thursday, saying the Wisconsin Department of Criminal Investigation into the officer-involved shooting must run its course. MADISON, Wis. — A Madison shooting involving a police officer from Wednesday afternoon is being considered an open and active homicide investigation. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway and Police Chief John Patterson spoke on the fatal shooting involving a police officer before being interrupted by protestors. A police officer shot and killed Corey Ruiz, who was in his 30s, on the city's near-east side Wednesday afternoon. Police alleged Ruiz was armed with a knife and injured one of the four officers who were trying to detain him. Prior to his death, Ruiz was seen "checking parked vehicles" in the Marquette neighborhood prior to the shooting, according to police. “It doesn't matter who you are, or what your past is. title: Wisconsin governor calls for transparency after officer kills man
text: Baltimore Sun eNewspaper Sign up for email newsletters Subscribe Login Sign up for email newsletters Baltimore Sun eNewspaper Don't miss: By SCOTT BAUER MADISON, Wis. (AP) — A police shooting death of a homeless man who the chief said wounded an officer with a knife while resisting arrest has roiled Wisconsin’s capital city, with protesters and community groups demanding accountability and an end to racial injustice. Corey Durell Ruiz, 38, was shot and killed on a city street Wednesday, the moments of his death captured in bystander videos that were later posted online. The race of the officer who fired his gun has not been released by police. Ruiz is identified as Black or Latino in Wisconsin court records. “It does not matter who you are or what your past is, you should not lose your life as a result of an encounter with law enforcement,” Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said during a news conference Thursday afternoon. Wisconsin court records show Ruiz had been in and out of jail over the past decade for mostly misdemeanor offenses including disorderly conduct, drug possession, auto theft, battery and invasion of privacy. He was also convicted of felonies including possession of cocaine and marijuana, robbery, strangulation, resisting an officer and causing bodily harm. “He’s a human being. He had a family. He has parents who loved him, who brought him home, who cared for him,” Common Council President Sabrina Madison said, adding that she’s struggling to understand what she’s seen in videos of the shooting that have circulated on social media. “My first thought is, when the officer’s walking away, why isn’t he walking away in cuffs?” Madison said. “I’m angry, there’s no way around it.” Ruiz’s family has retained Ben Crump, a prominent civil rights attorney, who said the case must be examined for excessive force. Frustrated residents marched, and a memorial of flowers and signs grew near the place where Ruiz died. It was just blocks from where two other police killings happened in 2015 and 2012. A group of about 20 protesters burst into Thursday’s news conference, taking the microphone from police Chief John Patterson and arguing with some attendees who said they wanted to hear more about the investigation. One protester held a sign saying “Corrupt cops deserve to die too!!!” Moments earlier, the mayor said the shooting would be “rigorously investigated.” Once the protesters quieted down, the chief resumed his presentation, promising his department’s full cooperation with the state investigation.  None of the four officers who were detaining Ruiz wore body cameras, but passersby recorded the confrontation on video, and accused the officers of overreacting. “I thought, ‘Holy cow — what could have warranted that?’ It looked to me like they had him under control,” David Ortiz-Whittingham, who saw officers swarming and heard the gunshots, said Thursday. “Even now, knowing about the knife, did he have to die for it? Could this have been de-escalated?” The police chief released few details Thursday, saying a Wisconsin Division of Criminal Investigation probe of the officer-involved shooting must run its course. Earlier Thursday, Madison’s independent police monitor, Aeiramique Glass, said police had not yet shared evidence or the officer’s identity with her office, which will review the case and can recommend to the district attorney that charges be filed if warranted. She said the department and city are “obstructing what the community and the public” want. “Let me do my job,” she said. Patterson said the police were committed to cooperating with Glass. Patterson has urged caution in reading too much from the cellphone videos. He said none show the perspective of the officers, and additional unreleased video was being reviewed. The officer who fired his weapon is an 11-year veteran of the force, the chief said. He and the three other responding officers will be placed on administrative leave. Patterson said police were responding to calls that someone was attempting to enter parked vehicles, and the suspect fled on a bike before the officers surrounded him. One deployed a taser, but Patterson said the effort failed to control the man. In the videos circulating online, the man can be seen standing before he’s brought to his knees as the officers struggle to force him into a prone position. Then he falls quickly to the pavement after what sounds like three gunshots, and seems motionless as the officers handcuff him behind his back. Arriving officers then escort one of the officers a short distance away. Patterson said he did not know the extent of the knife injuries sustained by the officer. “This situation was clearly dangerous,” Patterson said before adding he was saddened by the loss of life. The shooting happened in the middle of an intersection in the popular Marquette neighborhood, less than 2 miles (3.2 kilometers) from the state Capitol. Bystander videos show numerous cars at the scene, with people watching as it unfolds. “I saw everything! I saw everything! You did not need to kill him! … We watched it all!” a woman yells in the video recorded by Ortiz-Whittingham. Residents who dealt with two other police killings expressed frustration Thursday. In 2015, a white police officer shot and killed Tony Robinson, who was biracial, on the same street. Large protests followed, but the district attorney filed no charges, determining the officer was justified. In 2012, Paul Heenan, a white musician, was fatally shot after he had been drinking and mistakenly entered his neighbor’s house. That officer was exonerated as well. The chief acknowledged that the neighborhood “has experienced a lot of trauma” and urged people to support one another. “I want transparency. I want accountability,” Patterson said. Black advocacy groups, protesters and politicians are speaking out against the shooting, which has also focused attention on the Madison Police Department’s lack of body-worn cameras. The force of around 500 is among the largest in the Midwest that doesn’t use the devices. Madison, the Common Council president, said Thursday that she expects a police request for $400,000 to be approved, enabling the cameras to be phased in over the next three years. Others lamented that cameras weren’t already being used. The mayor said her budget, which has not yet been released, will include funding for body-worn cameras. Rhodes-Conway said the city needs to put together a policy for their use before the budget takes effect in January. The shooting has quickly infused itself into the race to succeed Gov. Tony Evers, who is not seeking a third term. Voting is already underway in the Aug. 11 primary. Democratic socialist candidate Francesca Hong called the shooting “state sanctioned violence.” Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley , a Democrat, said the reports are “painfully reminiscent of the tragedies we have witnessed in Kenosha, Minneapolis, and far too many communities.” Republican U.S. Rep. The police shooting death of a man who injured an officer with a knife while resisting arrest has roiled the city of Madison , Wisconsin , with Gov. Tony Evers calling for “transparency and accountability” in any investigation and community members gathering at a growing memorial for the man. Protesters marched Wednesday after the shooting and held a candlelight vigil for the man who died. Some even stayed at the growing memorial of candles, flowers and signs overnight, like Ben Weger. “I don't plan to leave anytime soon because it's important to hold this space,” said Weger, pastor of Stoughton United Methodist Church about 20 miles (32 kilometers) away. Sabrina Thompsen, of Madison, was crying at the memorial site. “It’s really unbearable,” she said. “You can’t describe it.” Evers posted online saying, “We will continue to keep the loved ones and family of the individual who was killed in our hearts and prayers.” “His life mattered,” the governor said. Cellphone video of the confrontation, where three gunshots could be heard, circulated on social media. Madison Police Chief John Patterson stressed at a news conference that the online footage was just one perspective of what happened. “I want to take a moment to honestly and sincerely offer my heartfelt sympathies to his family for this loss,” Patterson said. The man killed was in his 30s, Patterson said, but police did not release his name. Patterson said police were responding to calls that someone was attempting to enter parked vehicles in the neighborhood. The suspect fled on a bike in an attempt to get away before officers contacted him in the street. The suspect either fell off his bike or was taken off his bike by officers, Patterson said. During the struggle, the suspect pulled out a knife and injured an officer. An officer deployed a taser but it was unsuccessful. The same officer who was injured by the knife fired his weapon and the man who was shot died later at the hospital. The chief described the officer who fired his weapon as a veteran officer, but did not reveal any other details. Another officer was injured, but it is not clear how, Patterson said. Two other officers who were involved were uninjured. The Wisconsin Department of Criminal Investigation will investigate the shooting, and the four officers will be placed on administrative leave. “There are questions that must be answered,” Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway posted online. “It’s understandable that people want answers now.” The shooting happened on a city street in a popular neighborhood lined with restaurants, bars, shops and residential homes less than 2 miles (3.2 kilometers) from the state Capitol. Footage shows numerous cars stopped in the intersection with people watching as it unfolded. A white police officer shot and killed Tony Robinson , who was biracial, on the same street in 2015; a shooting that spurred large protests. The district attorney did not file charges against police in that case, determining the officer was justified. The race of the officer who fired his gun on Wednesday and that of the man killed were not released by police. But Black advocacy groups in Madison quickly spoke out against the crime and said they believed the man was Black. “Another Black man is dead on a Madison street, and our community watched him die before we even knew his name,” said Brandi Grayson, the head of the Madison-based Black community advocacy group Urban Triage. “That is the cruelty of state violence.” The shooting quickly infused itself into the Democratic race for governor, with one candidate addressing mourners at the site of the vigil Wednesday night and others calling for swift investigations. “I am horrified and devastated,” posted Francesca Hong, who showed up at the scene just a few blocks from her campaign office. Another candidate, County Executive David Crowley, said while details of what happened are still needed, “these reports are painfully reminiscent of the tragedies we have witnessed in Kenosha, Minneapolis, and far too many communities across our country.” A crowd had formed near where the shooting occurred on Wednesday with people chanting, “Arrest the cops!” They placed flowers and candles where the man was shot. Protesters also marched to the state Capitol and took the stage at a summer concert series, demanding the name of the officer and that he be held accountable. The Wisconsin Chamber Orchestra announced on social media the show was canceled. title: Protesters interrupt Madison news conference on officer - involved shooting , demanding answers
text: MADISON, Wis. (WMTV) - Madison leaders spent more than an hour on Thursday answering questions after Wednesday’s fatal officer-involved shooting that left a man named Corey Ruiz dead. The briefing, which began at 3 p.m., lasted almost two hours. The briefing was interrupted repeatedly as protestors demanded answers, shouting questions at city leaders and Madison Police Chief John Patterson before officials regained control and continued the briefing. While much of Thursday’s discussion focused on what happened before officers opened fire, city leaders also faced questions about what comes next and how the investigation will move forward. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway acknowledged there are still many questions about what led to the escalation, saying those answers will have to come through a thorough investigation. “As a city, as a community, as a society, we need to do better,” Mayor Rhodes-Conway said. “I want to be clear, it does not matter who you are, or what your past is, you should not lose your life as a result from an encounter with law enforcement.” As calls for accountability continued, Council President Sabrina Madison urged investigators to release information as quickly as possible and follow the evidence wherever it leads. Chief Patterson says the Wisconsin Department of Justice Division of Criminal Investigation is leading the homicide investigation and confirmed the officer involved will be publicly identified. The chief said the DOJ’s homicide investigation is the standard process in officer-involved deaths, and he declined to offer any opinion on the shooting while that investigation is underway. Anthony Cooper of Focused Interruption says we need to work together as a community, and that means talking to each other sensibly to de-escalate this conflict and future conflicts. “We have to make sure all voices are at the table,” Cooper said. “We have to also make sure that there is action that happens behind it, but the only way we’re able to do that is when we are having a conversation. It’s not you yelling at me, me yelling at you. We’re never going to get anywhere that way.” A vigil was being held on Thursday night. The Wisconsin Department of Justice’s Division of Criminal Investigation is reviewing the shooting and will later share the name of the officer who fatally shot Ruiz, which Patterson said he “sincerely hopes is soon.” “The more force we use, the less trust we have,” Patterson said during Thursday’s news conference. “That is the tension that we are living through right now in this city, and I can physically feel it.” Ruiz was in his 30s, Patterson said on Wednesday. His family has retained attorney Ben Crump, who is calling on authorities to preserve and release all footage of the incident, including squad-car and bystander video. “This case has to be examined for excessive force,” Crump said. “It happened in broad daylight, in front of dozens of witnesses. The family deserves the truth, and the public deserves accountability.” The confrontation has sparked outcry from protesters in a city that has previously been rocked by anger over police-involved shootings, a tension the police chief acknowledged Thursday during the news conference, saying, “We have to recognize the trauma that this community has gone through, is experiencing now again.” While Patterson addressed the room, a man from the crowd interrupted the news conference. The police chief offered to step aside and the protester approached the microphone, speaking for over 10 minutes as he expressed anger over the shooting. A woman stood next to him with a protest sign. “You’re going to say the same thing you all say every time a Black body gets shot down in this city. This is a corrupt city,” the man said. After the man gave Patterson the microphone back, the chief told the man: “I appreciate you being here. I know this is tough.” Rev. Marcus Allen, pastor at Mount Zion Baptist Church, also spoke at the news conference. “The emotions that that young man just presented here, that’s how all of us are really feeling,” Allen said. Like many deadly police-involved shootings in the past, questions around the shooting center on how much of a threat the officer faced, the lack of body-worn cameras and what can be seen in a bystander video. Police encountered Ruiz while responding to a report of a person checking parked vehicles Wednesday afternoon, Patterson said during a news conference Wednesday. On Thursday, a spokesperson for the police department said officers “were called to the area for someone stealing bicycles and checking vehicles.” Officers tried to make contact with him, but he fled on his bicycle through nearby backyards, according to police. When they caught up to him later near the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets on the city’s Near East Side, “a physical struggle ensued,” Patterson said. Ruiz pulled out a fixed-blade knife and injured one officer, described as a “veteran officer,” who was trying to arrest him, the chief added. “This was not a small, folding knife,” Patterson said. “It’s a large, fixed-blade knife.” Bystander video shows officers on the ground at an intersection, struggling with a man who is then pulled up to his feet. One officer can be heard yelling, “He’s got a knife,” while another yells “Taser! Taser! Taser,” deploying it as a police cruiser quickly pulls up. As the man begins to fall back to the ground and has his legs pinned by an officer’s foot, another officer appears to pull a gun, and three shots are heard. The officer who had drawn the Taser holds her hand to her mouth as she backs away. A different officer removes what appears to be a knife from the front of Ruiz’s body and tosses it on the ground behind him. title: Man dies after being shot by Madison Police Department officer
text: Warning: Videos in this article include the sound of gunshots and sounds of people reacting after the shooting. This video may be difficult to hear. MADISON, Wis. (WMTV) - A man has died after being shot by a Madison Police Department officer on Wednesday afternoon, the city’s chief of police confirmed. Madison Police Department Chief John Patterson said officers were dispatched around 1 p.m. for the report of a person checking through parked vehicles in the Marquette neighborhood. MPD officers found the man and tried to talk to him, and Patterson said the man allegedly rode away on his bike through nearby backyards. Officers found the man, who was in his 30s, at the intersection of Baldwin Street and Williamson Street around 1:30 p.m. Chief Patterson said the man either fell off or was removed from his bike by officers. A struggle happened with the man and officers, at which point Chief Patterson said the man allegedly pulled out a large knife. Patterson said an officer was injured by the knife while trying to arrest him. Police tried to use a taser on the man, which did not work. Chief Patterson said the officer who was injured by the knife was the same officer who then shot the man. Video submitted by a WMTV viewer contains three gunshots that can be heard. Officers performed lifesaving measures on the man before he was taken to a hospital, where he died. Officials said the man’s family has been notified. He was not named. “I want to take a moment to honestly and sincerely offer my heartfelt sympathies to his family for this loss,” Patterson said. In addition to the officer hurt by the knife, police said a second officer was also injured by something separately. The Wisconsin Department of Justice said both officers were treated at a hospital for their injuries and have been released. Four Madison Police Department officers were involved, and only one officer fired his weapon. The officer who fired his weapon is considered a veteran officer. Patterson did not name the officer who shot the man. The four officers involved were placed on administrative leave. Madison Police Department officers do not have body worn cameras. Chief Patterson said the police department has seen cell phone video circulating online of the shooting. “I will say that I am aware that cell phone video that has been shared and circulated online depicting this incident,” Chief Patterson said. “I ask the community recognize that there is other video that they have not seen that’s not circulating online that will be reviewed.” The Wisconsin Department of Justice Division of Criminal Justice is leading the investigation, with help from a DCI crime response specialist, Dane County Sheriff’s Office, Wisconsin State Patrol and Sun Prairie Police Department. Hundreds of people gathered on Williamson Street near where the shooting happened. Community members brought signs, chanted and shared their anger after the shooting. Many said this was an unfair situation. “The cops swarm him, tackle him, started trying to restrain him,” said David Ortiz-Whittingham, who witnessed the shooting. “I thought I saw him with his hands behind his back, but I’m not, you know, again it’s fuzzy, it’s the heat of the moment, it was all happening very fast.” Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway encouraged people to attend a community listening session on Thursday, which is being hosted by Common Council President Sabrina Madison. Chief Patterson will also attend, according to the City of Madison. Officials hope the event will connect community members directly with Madison leaders. People marched from Baldwin Street and Williamson Street to Capitol Square, where Concerts on the Square was taking place Wednesday night. Members of the crowd started to leave the event as a member of the group spoke out, demanding justice in the shooting. Protesters asked concert attendees to stand in support. Organizers canceled Concerts on the Square, thanking people for showing up to support music and saying they stand with the Black community. Nearby neighbors shut down the street with cones and caution tape to provide space for people to gather peacefully. People placed flowers and candles near the spot where the man was shot. The location of this deadly shooting is about a block and a half away from where police shot and killed Tony Robinson in March of 2015. The deadly shooting prompted a large community response, including walkouts and protests. The officer in that shooting was not charged for Robinson’s death. title: Realta Fusion will develop former Oscar Mayer site in Madison , add 600 jobs
text: Wisconsin Public Radio (WPR) Logo Donate Icon Donate Search wpr.org Search Icon Business Development , Economy , News , Nuclear Power , Science and Technology Realta Fusion will develop former Oscar Mayer site in Madison, add 600 jobs Company says it secured up to $55M in state, local development incentives A site that represents Madison’s industrial past will get new life as the host of a new research and development facility aimed at helping power the future. After a multi-state search, Realta Fusion selected OM Station, the site of the former Oscar Mayer plant and headquarters, to be its new corporate headquarters and research and development facility, the company announced Wednesday.  Realta Fusion is a Madison startup that formed in 2022, spinning out of work being done at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The company has approximately 50 employees in Madison and expects to eventually employ more than 600 people. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Realta plans to make $67 million worth of improvements to the portion of site that it will occupy, while the company’s equipment costs are estimated to be more than $500 million, according to a presentation from the city of Madison . To support the project, the company said it secured up to $55 million in incentives from both the state of Wisconsin and the city of Madison. That includes an estimated $37.5 million in sales and use tax exemptions, up to $15 million in state tax credits and $2.8 million in tax increment financing from the city, the company says. Before the end of the year, the company plans to break ground on the R&D facility, where it will build its prototype magnetic mirror fusion machine. Fusion generates power by fusing the atoms together to convert a small amount of mass into a large amount of energy. But the technology is still years away from being commercially viable, with Realta targeting the early to mid-2030s for its first commercial activities. Realta CEO Kieran Furlong said development incentives, local research expertise and a strong manufacturing base helped make the Badger State the best place for the company to continue growing. “Wisconsin has all the jigsaw pieces,” he told WPR. “We’ve got the leading R&D coming out of places like University of Wisconsin-Madison. We’ve got the manufacturing know-how in the core industrial centers around southeastern Wisconsin and up in the Fox River Valley. Wisconsin really has a chance to own the future of the fusion industry.” In addition to incentives, Furlong said the company also wanted to find a site with existing office and industrial buildings that could be repurposed and sites with strong electricity infrastructure and power availability. OM Station checked all those boxes. He said one of the biggest concerns when evaluating Wisconsin was its smaller talent pool compared with more populous states, but the strength of UW-Madison helped ease those concerns. “There’s already a wellspring of talent there in our respective fields of plasma physics, fusion, nuclear engineering and so on,” he said. “We’ve got that local pipeline of talent and know-how, and, so far, we’ve been very successful at attracting people to relocate to Wisconsin.” The project will bring new life to a property that has sat largely vacant since Kraft Heinz closed Oscar Mayer operations there in 2017 . The site served as a major manufacturing hub in Madison for nearly a century , helping shape the neighborhoods that grew around it. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said the city hopes Realta’s project can be a catalyst for additional development at the OM Station site. “Realta is proposing to take a significant chunk of the building and repurpose it for their use,” she said. “Having them there is a major attractor for businesses in their supply chain and other fusion-related businesses, and there is more room on that site that other businesses may be able to move into.” Officials say incentives, both at the state and local level, helped Wisconsin land the project and beat out other states, like New Jersey, Tennessee and Illinois. “Other states have equivalent incentive mechanisms and programs to attract and retain companies like ours, and we were courted hard by some of them,” Furlong said during a press conference Wednesday. “But when we compared state incentive packages apples to apples, Wisconsin simply made the most competitive offer.” In May, Realta was in the process of seeking financial incentives for sites in both Madison and Illinois, according to a memo from the city of Madison . Madison is offering Realta $2.8 million in tax increment financing tied to the creation or retention of 200 jobs and a $53 million boost in property value, according to city documents . TIF payments would be broken across six installments as the company hits job creation and property value benchmarks. The jobs listed in city documents have annual salaries ranging from $80,000 to more than $180,000. It’s the first time Madison has offered a tax increment financing for job creation in nearly a decade.  The city previously used jobs tax increment financing to support Exact Sciences in 2017 and 2018, according to the city’s presentation. “There’s always risk when we look to invest tax increment financing dollars, and that is something that we evaluate very carefully,” Rhodes-Conway said. “It’s part of why we’ve structured the deal to be a post-performance payment model, so they have to make their investment first, and they have to show that they’ve created jobs first.” On the state’s end, Realta estimates that it will receive $37.5 million in sales and use tax exemptions. Earlier this year, Gov. Tony Evers signed bipartisan legislation making Wisconsin the first in the nation to offer such incentives for fusion projects. During Wednesday’s press conference, Evers said the sales and use tax exemption for equipment purchases will help position Wisconsin as a national leader in the emerging fusion technology industry. “I’ll always be a science teacher at heart, so it excites me to think that — here in Wisconsin — we are engaging in groundbreaking research and applying it to real life issues,” Evers said. “That vision is what brings all of us here today and drives the fusion industry forward.” Realta said it expects to receive up to $15 million in state tax credits. Those credits generally require companies to meet investment and job creation requirements in order to receive the incentive. But Sam Rikkers, chief operating officer for the Wisconsin Economic Development Corp., declined to comment on those numbers, saying the agency did provide the company with a letter of support but the contract was still being finalized. Rikkers also said the company’s decision to continue growing in Wisconsin reflects the decades of investment in fusion at UW-Madison and recent state efforts. “Wisconsin is in pole position on the fusion industry and the fusion sector,” Rikkers said. “I really believe we’ll be leading this sector and all the things that come with it, not for a couple years, but for decades to come.” Wisconsin Public Radio, © Copyright 2026, Board of Regents of the University of Wisconsin System and Wisconsin Educational Communications Board. text: MADISON, Wis. (AP) — Protesters burst into a Thursday news conference about the police shooting of a homeless man in Madison, taking the microphone from the police chief and arguing with some attendees who said they wanted to hear more about the investigation. The group of roughly 20 protesters burst into the room at the Madison police station, shortly after Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway and Common Council President Sabrina Madison identified the man killed by police as Corey Durell Ruiz, a homeless resident. Ruiz, 38, was shot and killed Wednesday after police said he resisted arrest and injured an officer with a knife. Police Chief John Patterson stepped away from the microphone when the protesters were shouting, and one man in the group took his spot at the podium. The event quickly devolved into a shouting match. One protester held a sign saying “Corrupt cops deserve to die too!!!” Moments earlier, the mayor said the shooting will be “rigorously investigated.” “It does not matter who you are or what your past is, you should not lose your life as a result of an encounter with law enforcement,” Satya Rhodes-Conway said. Madison, for her part, said “Corey could have been my brother because my brother is homeless and he often rides a bike.” Court records show Ruiz had been in and out of jail over the past decade on charges including failing to pay child support, driving a vehicle without consent, jumping bail, threatening authorities, taking a vehicle without consent, possessing drug paraphernalia, resisting an officer and retail theft. “He’s a human being. He had a family. He has parents who loved him who brought him home, who cared for him,” Madison said, adding that she’s struggling to understand what she’s seen in videos of the shooting that have circulated on social media. “My first thought is, when the officer’s walking away, why isn’t he walking away in cuffs,” Madison said. “I’m angry, there’s no way around it.” Once the protesters quieted down, the chief resumed his presentation, promising his department’s full cooperation with the state investigation. The shooting has roiled Wisconsin’s capital city, with Gov. Tony Evers calling for “transparency and accountability” and Madison community members gathering Thursday at a growing memorial. None of the four officers who were detaining the man wore body cameras, but passersby recorded the confrontation on video, and accused the officers of overreacting. “I thought, ‘Holy cow — what could have warranted that?’ It looked to me like they had him under control,” David Ortiz-Whittingham, who saw officers swarming and heard the gunshots, said Thursday. “Even now, knowing about the knife, did he have to die for it? Could this have been de-escalated without him losing his life?” The police chief released few details Thursday, saying the Wisconsin Department of Criminal Investigation into the officer-involved shooting must run its course. Earlier Thursday, Madison’s independent police monitor, Aeiramique Glass, said police have not yet shared evidence or the officer’s identity with her office, which will review the case and can recommend to the district attorney that charges be filed if warranted. She said the department and city are “obstructing what the community and the public” want. “Let me do my job,” she said. Patterson said the police were committed to cooperating with Glass as the independent monitor’s investigation is carried out, at the same time as the state’s probe. (AP) — The Madison police officer who shot and killed Corey Ruiz should face criminal charges, civil rights attorney Ben Crump said Friday, after protests erupted in anger over videos of their struggle. “They not only tackled him, not only tased him, not only kicked him, but you saw they shot him three times in his head and other parts of his body,” Crump said . He spoke at an emotional news conference with Ruiz’s mother, siblings and 13-year-old daughter, Kah’liyah Aliomar. Ruiz, 38, was killed on a busy city street Wednesday, just a couple of blocks away from his daughter’s home and along the route she walks to school. Police say Ruiz pulled a knife during a struggle with four officers, injuring one of them. That officer then fired the shots, according to police. All four officers have been placed on administrative leave pending a state investigation, and the officer who fired the shots has not yet been identified. Aliomar cried as she described learning of her father’s death. “My heart was broken and hurt so much knowing I can’t see my father anymore,” she said. His mother Elsa Ruiz said she never imagined she would have to bury her son. “He was my love. He loved his daughter, he loved his family. He did not deserve to be taken out like that. They took my baby from me,” she said, sobbing. The family promised to seek justice for Ruiz’s death, which Crump called an unjustified “execution.” “Anytime there is excessive use of force, there should be accountability,” Crump said. He said it was “shocking on every level.” The shooting was captured on cellphone video that was widely shared online, though Madison Police Chief John Patterson cautioned Thursday that the video did not show the altercation from the police officers’ perspective. But unlike nearly every other similarly sized city, Madison doesn’t require its police to use body-worn cameras, so there is no footage from the officers’ perspective. Over the last decade city officials have repeatedly debated adopting the cameras — at times creating subcommittees and doing studies on the idea — but local officials have primarily blamed budget concerns and political inertia for the ongoing stalemate.  Another common source of opposition, identified in a 2021 feasibility study , came from community groups worried the cameras would be used to surveil and criminalize marginalized groups. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said Thursday that she expects the new budget that takes effect in January to include funding for body-worn cameras. “Thank God there was video,” Crump said. “If there wasn’t video, imagine what the narrative would have been.” Wisconsin court records show Ruiz had been in and out of jail over the past decade for mostly misdemeanor offenses including disorderly conduct, drug possession, auto theft, battery and invasion of privacy. He was also convicted of felonies including possession of cocaine and marijuana, robbery, strangulation, resisting an officer and causing bodily harm. “People are saying he’s a criminal. So what? He had a family, he had me,” Aliomar said, breaking down into tears. Police said they were at the street to investigate reports that someone was trying to enter parked cars, something Crump said amounted to only the suspicion of a low-level property crime. “I need somebody to help me understand why they felt it was OK to execute my brother based on no facts at all,” Veronica Ruiz said. “I hope everyone continues to support and come together and find justice for him.” The police chief has released few details about the shooting. Patterson said Thursday that a Wisconsin Division of Criminal Investigation probe must run its course. A separate investigation by the city’s independent police monitor is also underway. “The situation was clearly dangerous,” Patterson said, and that he did not know the extent of the knife injuries sustained by the officer. He also said he wanted transparency and accountability in the investigation. The killing sparked protests, calls for justice from elected officials and anger from a community where police have killed three people in the same neighborhood since 2012. The package includes $37.5 million in newly created sales and use tax exemptions for commercial fusion companies, up to $15 million in performance-based enterprise zone tax credits from WEDC, the state’s economic development agency, and $2.8 million in staggered tax increment financing targeted at job growth from Madison, which the city council unanimously approved in June. “Madison does not take the decision to provide tax increment financing lightly, but this was the right kind of project for the city to support,” said Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway. “This is an opportunity to bring hundreds of high-paying jobs in the sustainable energy sector to our community and revitalize a largely vacant property that means so much to Madisonians.” Ald. Julia Matthews, whose district includes the Oscar Mayer site at 910 Mayer Ave., says she’s received under a dozen emails from constituents over the project, largely split between enthusiasm and concerns over nuclear research in general, and the potential for contamination from tritium, a hydrogen isotope used as fusion fuel that’s weakly radioactive and can’t penetrate human skin. (Furlong says they will not use tritium on-site— the Hammir will only use a non-radioactive isotope called deuterium, or “heavy water.”) Matthews says Realta answered concerns “as good as they could have,” and met with the Sherman Neighborhood Association to explain the project. “ I do really believe this is going to be a great opportunity for the Oscar Mayer area, with the potential job growth,” she adds. Furlong says Realta ramped up conversations on incentives starting in the latter half of 2025, and says credit goes to those officials who “see the potential,” and recognize Wisconsin’s “comparative advantage in fusion” based on decades of research at UW-Madison. The enterprise zone credits, he says, are a “seed investment” for “one of the biggest industries of the 21st century.” Furlong, like other boosters, sees fusion energy as an ecosystem that could drive future economic activity and tap into Wisconsin’s manufacturing base. “There’s a lot of machinery that needs to be made for these fusion power plants, and the state of Wisconsin is extremely well-placed to deliver on those,” he says, adding that nuclear fusion could be to Madison what the auto industry was to Detroit. Today, Realta’s workforce is dominated by physicists and engineers. The company has hired about 45 people and expects to hire roughly 600 more in their next phase. Furlong expects that before long, fusion could rise all boats, and bring in more skilled tradespeople — technicians, welders and more. "I often talk about knocking the rust off the Rust Belt,” he says, predicting “a lot of work for a lot of people in the region.” Courtesy Realta Fusion A rendering of Realta Fusion's soon-to-be-new-digs on the site of the former Oscar Mayer plant. Realta is currently based in Madison, with administrative offices on the west side on John Q Hammons Drive and a research facility shared with UW-Madison in Stoughton, where their current prototype, WHAM, is located. The WHAM is a large, long cylinder with powerful magnets on either side. At OM Station, Realta will be hammering away at their next fusion prototype: the “Hammir.” The Hammir won’t be used as a power plant. It will need electricity rather than generate it, and having available power hookups was one reason the site was attractive. The Hammir will look like the WHAM. But it will have a second pair of powerful magnets, a set-up Realta calls a “tandem mirror” design. Furlong says the goal is to demonstrate the plasma conditions and magnetic field strength the company believes will be needed for commercial power plants in the future “that we’ll build out across the world.” The cylinder design of both is unlike many other models used in nuclear fusion experiments, which more commonly use a donut-shaped design called a “tokamak.” But the WHAM’s cylinder shape, says Furlong, gives Realta more flexibility to experiment with something called “ direct energy conversion ” — a way of more efficiently converting plasma energy directly into electricity. Direct energy conversion is something Realta demonstrated on an Isthmus visit to the WHAM — it only generated enough energy for a lightbulb. Furlong says that was just “showing what’s possible” for the future, but was an important proof of concept in making fusion energy efficient. But the future is what Furlong is laser-focused on. To demonstrate, he holds up a clear glass tumbler. If this glass had heavy water instead of the regular stuff, he says, it would be more than enough to fulfill his lifetime energy needs many times over using fusion energy. “It’s really important to understand. You need a very tiny amount of fuel for a fusion power plant,” Furlong says. He’s determined to make fusion energy not just possible, but cheap and scalable, so it can be used as a realistic alternative to fossil fuels. “It’s not just enough to make fusion work,” says Furlong. “We have to make sure we can make electricity cost-effective.” by Chali Pittman July 15, 2026 7:02 AM ISTHMUS is © 2026 Isthmus Community Media, Inc. | All rights reserved. | Madison, Wisconsin | USA To submit an event to Isthmus, please send an email with the following information to calendar@isthmus.com Here's the information we need to include your event in our calendar: * event/performer/speaker name * brief description/music genre/etc. * start and end time * event date; RSVP/ticket deadline if there is one * venue/location * cover charge/price * contact phone number, email or website we can publish (REQUIRED)  Optional info: * bios/press releases for posting with the online listing

title: Candidates for Wisconsin governor react to Madison shooting
text: Wisconsin Public Radio (WPR) Logo Donate Icon Donate Search wpr.org Search Icon Elections , Law enforcement , News , Politics Candidates for Wisconsin governor react to Madison shooting Democrats call for a thorough review and body cameras for Madison police. Rep. Francesca Hong called the shooting an 'execution.' Democrats running to be Wisconsin’s next governor and Republican frontrunner Tom Tiffany are calling for a swift, transparent and independent investigation into the Madison police shooting of 38-year-old Corey Ruiz. The shooting on Williamson Street in Madison has sparked protests at the state Capitol and renewed anger toward police. In the same neighborhood, Madison officers fatally shot unarmed Black teenager Tony Robinson in 2015 and 30-year-old white musician Paul Heenan in 2012. Madison Police Chief John Patterson has said police were trying to apprehend Ruiz, who pulled a knife and injured an officer. That officer then shot Ruiz. Court records show Ruiz has a history of criminal convictions and had pleaded guilty in 2021 to a felony charge of resisting arrest in a way that caused bodily harm to police. Democrats said they felt sorrow for Ruiz’s family. On Wednesday, Madison Rep. Francesca Hong, who has been leading in the Democratic primary race, said she was horrified when she saw video of the incident and called the shooting an “ execution .” “In responding to a mental health crisis where clearly the individual did not need to be apprehended, I think the video speaks for itself,” Hong told WPR Thursday. “That was an incorrect response, and no one should be dead right now. Again, another Black man is dead.” Hong said there should be multiple reviews and an examination of training and body cameras. Madison police don’t currently have department-wide body cameras, but Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said in a Thursday press conference that she would request funding for body cameras in her next budget. Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who reentered the Democratic primary July 18 after Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez dropped out, told WPR that the investigation should be allowed to play out. Crowley said he’s curious to hear the officer’s reasons for shooting Ruiz and police accounts of the incident, adding that he wanted to ensure people’s rights to protest are respected. He said such situations can bring up trauma for residents and referenced the murder of George Floyd by Derek Chauvin, the former Minneapolis police officer. He also mentioned the shooting of Jacob Blake by Kenosha police officer Rusten Sheskey. “A governor’s role in a moment like this is to bring people together, to recognize that, you know, this is not only a loss to Madison, but this is a loss to the entire state,” Crowley said. “We got to figure out ways that we put policies, procedures, and standard operating procedures in place that, you know, stops these things from happening in the future.” Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes called the shooting distressing and disturbing. He highlighted people’s concerns about the lack of body cameras among Madison police, demanding accountability. “The video is bad, but I do want to make sure that, you know, we are also being very thorough in the way that it is investigated. Accountability on the other end means if there was wrongdoing, actual nefarious actions, then there should be prosecution,” Barnes said Thursday. “One of the problems is typically it has been too easy for officers to get away with that sort of behavior. Six years ago, with the wave of resistance to violence, if anything that we learned from that is that this is not acceptable.” Former Department of Administration Secretary Joel Brennan said Thursday there needs to be “sober judgment” in times like these while echoing the call to protect people’s rights to exercise free speech. Brennan added there needs to be an appropriate level of training with an emphasis on de-escalation in such incidents. He also said most money for law enforcement comes through state aid known as shared revenue, but funding for police and fire and emergency services largely stems from raising property taxes . “There needs to be appropriate accountability, but there also needs to be the appropriate level of investment there…. There should be more funding for state shared revenue for local units of government all around the state,” Brennan said. “Madison is, I think, one of the lower recipients of state shared revenue in the state. But, no matter what, those resources are important to ensuring that everything can be done in the right way at the local level.” Madison state Sen. Kelda Roys said it’s impossible to imagine any justification for how the shooting occurred, saying that Ruiz and his loved ones deserve justice. She said the nation has seen a pattern and “level of police violence that is intolerable,” citing an unwillingness to tackle illegal guns and gun safety as one of the reasons. “If you don a badge and carry a gun at your job, then you should be meeting the highest standard. And so, you know, education and training is part of it, but culture is also a part of it,” Roys said. “And making sure that law enforcement officers are both safe on their job, which they absolutely have a right to be, but we also have a right to be safe in our community.” In a statement on social media , Tiffany said any loss of life is tragic and offered prayers for all involved in the shooting. During his time in the Legislature, he said Wisconsin established the nation’s first statewide law requiring independent investigators for police-involved deaths, saying politicians shouldn’t rush to judgment. “Too many politicians rush to the cameras before the facts are even known. Francesca Hong chose to do that (Wednesday), declaring to a crowd, ‘This state sanctioned violence was an execution,’” Tiffany wrote. “As governor, I will lead Wisconsin with a steady hand, let the facts guide accountability, and work to end revolving-door criminal justice policies.” Andy Manske, the other Republican running for governor, said in a statement to WPR that all life lost is a great lost, and that many questions remained, including why Madison had resisted body cameras. “It is indisputable that body cameras have been opposed by the local government,” Manske said. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Manske also criticized Hong for her remarks, saying they had made the situation “far more risky to citizens.” The names of the officer who fired shots and other officers involved in Wednesday’s shooting have not yet been released. title: Irate protesters commandeer Madison shooting news conference , police chief pledges cooperation with investigation
text: To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video MADISON, Wis. (CBS 58) — Tensions in Madison escalated Thursday afternoon, July 23, as city and police leaders held another news conference about the fatal police shooting of a man the day before . The briefing was interrupted several times by protesters. It was a surreal scene at Madison Police Department headquarters as the situation threatened to boil over. A protester commandeered the microphone from the police chief, berated him and other officials, then held the floor for more than 15 minutes as city leaders stood by and watched. CBS 58 While the police chief pledged transparency throughout the independent investigation, many people remained skeptical. About 20 minutes into the news conference, Carlos Dixon — a self-described activist and fringe candidate for governor — started shouting questions from the back of the room. He yelled at Madison Police Chief John Patterson, "We can shut this down. You can stop talking because we don't want to hear anything you've been saying." He continued, "We have the power! Not that badge, not that weapon! We have the power!" Dixon then approached Patterson at the podium. "Give me this microphone, then. Excuse me." An irate Dixon took over the news conference, railing against the police department over the shooting. "If it had been my Black ass that murdered somebody in the street, y'all'd have me in jail right now!" Dixon said. When other community members wanted to hear the police chief's explanation, Dixon turned on them. For more than 15 minutes, Dixon and others disrupted the news conference as Patterson, Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway and others stood by. Eventually, tensions cooled slightly, and Dixon walked to the back of the room. Patterson then resumed his comments. "I appreciate you being here. I know this is tough," Patterson said. "I think everyone in this room can feel the thinness of trust in the city right now." Patterson said the Wisconsin Department of Criminal Investigation is leading the independent investigation into the shooting. He said his department will cooperate fully and will not interfere with the investigation. He also declined to offer an opinion on the shooting so as not to jeopardize the investigation's independence. "This process exists precisely so that no department in the state investigates itself," Patterson said. Other community members also spoke, including Dr. Marcus Allen Sr., senior pastor at Mt. Zion Baptist Church. "The emotions that that young man just presented here, that's how all of us are really feeling," Allen said. The investigation will rely in part on cellphone videos circulating on social media because the Madison Police Department does not have body cameras. "This has been a conversation that our community has been having for a very long time," Rhodes-Conway said. The police chief and the department have requested body cameras in the past, but the Common Council previously voted against funding them. Common Council President Alder Sabrina Madison said the issue is complicated because previous funding priorities included shelters and other community projects. This time, Madison said the support appears to be there. "I have not heard that any alders don't support body-worn cameras this year," she said. Rhodes-Conway said her next budget proposal will include funding for a body camera program. CBS 58 The officer who shot Corey Ruiz has not been identified. Patterson said he hopes the DCI investigation will lead to the officer's name being released soon. Patterson said he was told the officer suffered a knife injury during the confrontation, but he has not personally seen the injuries or spoken with the officer.

title: Francesca Hong , leftist candidate for Wisconsin governor , called 911 on anti - Israeli protester in 2023 , report says
text: About Locations Advertise Subscribe Share Source: francescahong.com Politics • Jul 7, 2026, 11:03 AM CT Democratic candidate for governor Francesca Hong, the leftist in the race, called 911 on an anti-Israeli protest display in 2023, according to a report from the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel .  The democratic socialist and frontrunner in the primary reported a protest display featuring a paint-splattered Israeli flag — a decision she told the outlet she regrets.  In late December 2023, Hong called Madison police twice to report a “highly antisemitic act” that she wanted to be “potentially investigated as a hate crime,” according to the police report obtained by the Journal Sentinel.  Hong, who represents part of downtown Madison as a member of the State Assembly, was sent a photograph of the protest display featuring an Israeli flag and fake bodies splattered with red paint.  Portions of Hong’s calls to police have been posted to TikTok in recent months. “Three years ago, there was a piece of protest art at the encampments in Madison, which was photographed and posted to social media,” Hong said in a statement. “My constituents reported they felt threatened and alerted me to the social post, but the image was cropped and incomplete to misrepresent anti-Zionism as antisemitism – a distinction I take seriously. “Based on their concerns for their safety and my incomplete information, I did something I regret deeply: I called the police and asked them to look into it. This turned out to be a mistake because the image posted to social media was intentionally misleading. I believe in free speech. I support a free Palestine. The genocide in Gaza and the colonization of the West Bank must end.” Hong also texted Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway about the display, according to the report. Records also include a call to the non-emergency line from former Madison Ald. MGR Govindarajan, who represented the area on the City Council. Hong told the police dispatcher that she was not at the site of the display but said she received a photo of it. She said she was “trying to figure out what the fastest way to take it down is because I’m not at the location.” The dispatcher said he would have an officer look into it, but “I don’t know legally if officers can force somebody to take this down.” Hong asked if it could be removed because it was on city property, and then said she’d like it to be investigated as a potential hate crime. The dispatcher said officers would first need to investigate whether a crime was committed. In a second call, Hong again described the display to another dispatcher as “a display of antisemitism that’s pretty disturbing and jarring.” The officer following up on the call wrote in his report: “The display was removed subsequent to my taking Hong’s call after approximately an hour and a half in which she had contacted the Madison police again to report that she had received numerous phone calls from constituents in the Madison area advising her of the uncouth nature of the display in question.” After police removed the display, its creator and owner, Jesse Ransom, contacted police because he had previously put a GPS tracker on it and could see that it was moving. Ransom tried to report the removal as a theft, arguing he’d taken steps to comply with city rules. Ransom said he built the beginning of the display early in December 2023 as part of an ongoing protest action to urge U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin to call for a ceasefire after the Oct. 7 Hamas attack on Israel and Israel’s subsequent retaliation – which she ultimately did Dec. 21. Ransom said he first parked his bike with the display downtown on Dec. 15. On Dec. 22, he said, he added items to the display like the Israeli flag “with red paint to symbolize blood being spilled in war.” Ransom has voiced frustration that none of the police reports related to his bike include the fact that the word “CEASEFIRE” was painted on it, along with a phone number to contact Baldwin. “While exercising my first amendment rights to petition my government and complying with all laws my private property was unlawfully seized by Madison Police department without due process for political speech,” Ransom wrote in a complaint filed with the police over the incident. Ransom confronted Hong about the incident during an event in June 2024 and later shared a recording of their conversation with the Journal Sentinel. “I did not know there was a ‘ceasefire now’ sign,” Hong told Ransom. She said the campaign staffer who informed her about the incident was “deeply upset” and that she also heard from “community members who agreed that it was something we should try to take down.” Ransom responded that the display was “free speech directed at Tammy Baldwin,” to which Hong replied, “Absolutely.” Hong acknowledged her regret over the incident, telling Ransom, “I regret calling the police. I regret having that taken down.” She said she had sought to make amends through her subsequent actions, including introducing a resolution calling for a ceasefire in Gaza and sponsoring legislation to repeal Wisconsin’s anti-BDS law. The law, enacted under former Gov. Scott Walker, prohibits state and local governments from participating in boycotts of Israel. During Wisconsin’s spring 2024 election, Hong was among the elected officials who helped lead the state’s “uninstructed” campaign, which encouraged voters to protest the Biden administration’s military aid to Israel and call for a ceasefire in Gaza. Hong also emerged as a leading opponent of legislation signed by Gov. Tony Evers in March that codified the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s 2016 definition of “antisemitism” for use by state and local governments. Critics of the measure argued that it could infringe on free speech rights. Madison Police Department Chief John Patterson said the killing of Ruiz is “an open active homicide investigation,” adding that the “Madison Police Department has called for a thorough and independent criminal investigation into yesterday’s shooting.” “It does not matter who you are or what your past is. You should not lose your life as a result of an encounter with law enforcement,” Rhodes-Conway said during a news conference Thursday. The Wisconsin Department of Justice’s Division of Criminal Investigation is reviewing the shooting and will later share the name of the officer who fatally shot Ruiz, which Patterson said he “sincerely hopes is soon.” “The more force we use, the less trust we have,” Patterson said during Thursday’s news conference. “That is the tension that we are living through right now in this city, and I can physically feel it.” Ruiz was in his 30s, Patterson said on Wednesday. His family has retained attorney Ben Crump, who is calling on authorities to preserve and release all footage of the incident, including squad-car and bystander video. “This case has to be examined for excessive force,” Crump said. “It happened in broad daylight, in front of dozens of witnesses. The family deserves the truth, and the public deserves accountability.” The confrontation has sparked outcry from protesters in a city that has previously been rocked by anger over police-involved shootings, a tension the police chief acknowledged Thursday during the news conference, saying, “We have to recognize the trauma that this community has gone through, is experiencing now again.” While Patterson addressed the room, a man from the crowd interrupted the news conference. The police chief offered to step aside and the protester approached the microphone, speaking for over 10 minutes as he expressed anger over the shooting. A woman stood next to him with a protest sign. “You’re going to say the same thing you all say every time a Black body gets shot down in this city. This is a corrupt city,” the man said. After the man gave Patterson the microphone back, the chief told the man: “I appreciate you being here. I know this is tough.” Rev. Marcus Allen, pastor at Mount Zion Baptist Church, also spoke at the news conference. “The emotions that that young man just presented here, that’s how all of us are really feeling,” Allen said. Shooting captured on video as police urge patience Like many deadly police-involved shootings in the past, questions around the shooting center on how much of a threat the officer faced, the lack of body-worn cameras and what can be seen in a bystander video. Police encountered Ruiz while responding to a report of a person checking parked vehicles Wednesday afternoon, Patterson said during a news conference Wednesday. On Thursday, a spokesperson for the police department said officers “were called to the area for someone stealing bicycles and checking vehicles.” Officers tried to make contact with him, but he fled on his bicycle through nearby backyards, according to police. When they caught up to him later near the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets on the city’s Near East Side, “a physical struggle ensued,” Patterson said. Ruiz pulled out a fixed-blade knife and injured one officer, described as a “veteran officer,” who was trying to arrest him, the chief added. “This was not a small, folding knife,” Patterson said. “It’s a large, fixed-blade knife.” Bystander video shows officers on the ground at an intersection, struggling with a man who is then pulled up to his feet. One officer can be heard yelling, “He’s got a knife,” while another yells “Taser! Taser! Taser,” deploying it as a police cruiser quickly pulls up. As the man begins to fall back to the ground and has his legs pinned by an officer’s foot, another officer appears to pull a gun, and three shots are heard. The officer who had drawn the Taser holds her hand to her mouth as she backs away. title: Protests erupt in Madison , Wisconsin following police execution of Corey Ruiz
